ch1-coins.title: Find when the two coins always agree
ch1-coins.breaks: Real coins have a hidden answer from the start. Bell pairs do not. You also cannot send a message with them, because each side alone only sees random results.

levels.kid: Which dial settings could make the two coins agree every time?
levels.student: Compare two runs: both cities on the same dial, then the two cities on different dials.

levels.kid: Coins asked the same question give the same answer.
levels.student: When both cities measure in the same basis, their results match every time. Run the flips with both dials on Z, then both on X.

levels.kid: Put both dials on the same letter and flip. Then put them on different letters and flip again.
levels.student: Same basis should give 20 agreements out of 20. Z against X should give about 10, and the 10 change from run to run. The two dial controls are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the table fill in for both dial settings, one after the other.
levels.student: The page runs 20 flips with Z and Z, then 20 with Z and X. Your own runs stay in the table so you can compare.

levels.kid: Same letters always agree, and different letters agree about half the time, like tossing a fair coin.
levels.student: For the pair (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, equal bases give equal results every time. Mixed bases give independent 50/50 results.

ch2-links.title: See how many seats a road gets in 30 rounds
ch2-links.breaks: Real attempts take time and hardware. Here a whole round happens in one step.

levels.kid: If each plane lands 8 times out of 10, how many of 6 planes would you expect to land?
levels.student: Expected seats are M times q. Try q = 0.8 and compare the tallest bar with that number.

levels.kid: Each road throws 6 planes, and each plane lands on its own.
levels.student: The seats on one road follow Binomial(6, q), so the tallest bars sit near 6 times q.

levels.kid: Set the slider to 0.8, press Run 30 rounds, and look for the tallest blue bar.
levels.student: At q = 0.8 the exact bars peak at 5 seats (about 0.39) and 6 seats (about 0.26). With only 120 roads in the run, the blue bars wobble around the outlined bars. The slider is outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the page throw 30 rounds of planes and count the seats on each road.
levels.student: The page runs 30 rounds with a fixed seed. Compare each blue bar with the outlined exact bar next to it.

levels.kid: The page ran 30 rounds, and the blue bars land near the outlined ones.
levels.student: Each road's seats follow Binomial(6, q), so with more rounds the blue bars settle onto the outlined bars.

ch3-swap.title: Make cities A and D share a pair they can use
ch3-swap.breaks: The middle city's coins are used up by the join. The end pair is unusable until the phone call arrives.

levels.kid: After B joins its two coins, can A and D use their pair right away?
levels.student: Think about what A and D still do not know about the joined result.

levels.kid: B has to tell A and D how the join turned out.
levels.student: The swap is a Bell-state measurement at B. Its outcome is a classical message that A and D need before they can fix their qubits.

levels.kid: Press Join at B first. Then press Phone A and D.
levels.student: The join is a quantum step at B. The phone call is the classical step, and the arc stays grey until it arrives. The two buttons are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch B join, then watch the message travel to A and D.
levels.student: The page does the join, then sends the classical message from B to both ends. The arc turns usable only after the message arrives.

levels.kid: B joined its two coins, then phoned A and D, and now their pair is usable.
levels.student: A and D needed B's measurement result to correct their qubits, so the pair counted only after the call.

ch4-fidelity.title: Add middle cities until the meter turns red
ch4-fidelity.breaks: The grey is random noise, not a copy, because quantum states cannot be copied. Real swaps also add noise of their own, which this model ignores.

levels.kid: How many middle cities do you think a pair can pass through before it is too washed out?
levels.student: Each swap lowers fidelity. Guess where the meter crosses the line at 0.78.

levels.kid: Every join mixes in a little grey paint.
levels.student: Fidelity falls with each link as F_L = (3 w^L + 1) / 4, so the meter drops fast once there are several links.

levels.kid: Keep pressing Add a middle city and watch the number and the line.
levels.student: With F = 0.95, the path has L links, one more than the middle cities. L = 5 still gives 0.78 or more, and L = 6 gives 0.75. The Add button is outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the page add cities one at a time until the meter turns red.
levels.student: The page adds middle cities until the fidelity drops below 0.78, which happens at 5 middle cities.

levels.kid: Four middle cities are fine, and the fifth one washes the pair out.
levels.student: With F = 0.95, 5 links give 0.781 and 6 links give 0.746, so the limit at f = 0.78 is 4 middle cities.

ch5-rush.title: Serve as many requests as the best possible answer
ch5-rush.breaks: A pair is never cut in half. Each pair travels whole, on a single route.

levels.kid: Which road has the fewest seats, and which request needs it?
levels.student: A request needs its pairs on every link of its route, so look at the weakest link first.

levels.kid: A road can carry only as many pairs as its weakest link.
levels.student: A route's capacity is the smallest seat count along it. When one road is not enough, split the request over roads that share no link.

levels.kid: Draw the request with the fewest options first, and read what the referee says.
levels.student: The shortest roads often take seats another request needs. Try a longer road for a request that has spare choices. The cities of the request you are drawing are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the best answer drawn in green, with your roads still on screen.
levels.student: The green roads come from the exact solver, qmp.ilp.solve_path, run on this instance in the current mode.

levels.kid: The best answer is drawn for you, and it serves as many requests as any legal answer can.
levels.student: The exact solver tries every legal choice of roads, so no answer under these rules serves more requests.

fig1-walk.title: Predict the walk, then step through it
fig1-walk.breaks: The paper prints alpha 3 as 4/2, but the rule that matches its other values gives 3/2. The chosen path does not change.

levels.kid: From city 7, which neighbour looks best, the one with the better seats-per-step score?
levels.student: Compare the score for city 1 with the score for city 8: the larger fraction wins.

levels.kid: Each neighbour gets a score: seats on the bottleneck, divided by steps to go.
levels.student: alpha_i = min(seats on link k-i, best bottleneck from i to the destination) divided by the hops from i. The walk picks the largest alpha.

levels.kid: City 1 scores 4/3 and city 8 scores 4/2. Which fraction is larger?
levels.student: 4/2 is 2 and 4/3 is about 1.33, so the walk goes to city 8. The two neighbours of city 7 are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the walk go one step at a time, with the scores shown.
levels.student: Step through the walk in the table of scores. The chosen neighbour is marked at each step.

levels.kid: The walk goes 7, 8, 5, 6 first, then 7, 1, 2, 4, 6 second, and splits the 4 pairs as 2 and 2.
levels.student: Each path has a bottleneck of 4 seats, and the spare-seat rule lets a request use half of them, which is 2 pairs per path.
